title: Origins and History of Baldwin Sharknose
body:
The Baldwin Sharknose belongs to the 1950–1953 era and traces to Baldwin.

Stockton & Darlington (1825) and Rainhill (1829, Rocket) proved steam railways; America built 30,000 miles by 1860 and joined coasts at Promontory in 1869. The 4-4-0 American standardized the frontier; the 2-8-0 Consolidation hauled freight; superpower (Berkshire, 1925) and the Big Boy (1941) were steam's apex. Interurbans and streetcars (1880s–1920s) electrified cities; Pullman (1865+) made travel comfortable; streamliners (1934, Burlington Zephyr) fought the Depression with speed. Diesels (FT, 1939) killed steam by the 1950s; mergers consolidated the map. Telegraph block signals and train orders kept it safe — mostly.

Within that longer story, Baldwin Sharknose: The 1950; the 1953's. The Sharknose is the Baldwin's snout.

title: How Baldwin Sharknose Works
body:
Steam locomotives boil water in a fire-tube boiler; steam drives pistons connected to driving wheels via side rods; the fireman feeds coal (or oil), the engineer works throttle, reverser (Johnson bar), and air brakes (Westinghouse, 1869). Adhesion limits tractive effort (~25% of driver weight); sand helps. Signaling evolved from timetable-and-train-order to automatic block signals (semaphore, then color-light); CTC centralized control. Streetcars drew 600V DC from overhead wire via trolley pole; interurbans ran faster on private right-of-way.

Applied to the Baldwin Sharknose (1950–1953, Baldwin): The Sharknose is the Baldwin's snout.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Railroad History Glossary

The working vocabulary of railroad history:

• Whyre/Whyte notation — 2-8-0 etc.: leading/drivers/trailing wheels.
• tractive effort — Pull at the drawbar; the locomotive's muscle.
• adhesion — Friction limit; ~25% of weight on drivers.
• superpower — 1920s big-firebox, high-horsepower steam.
• streamliner — Diesel-powered speed trains of the 1930s.
• interurban — Electric intercity railway; the first commuter rail.
• caboose — Crew car; the conductor's office.
• Pullman — Sleeping/dining luxury; the porter era.
• train order — Written authority to occupy track.
• block signal — Track divided into protected sections.
• CTC — Centralized traffic control; the dispatcher's panel.
• railfan — The enthusiast; foamers chase steam.

title: Baldwin Sharknose — Tractive effort + train dynamics (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes tractive effort from cylinder dimensions, grade resistance, and stopping distance — the operating department's physics.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Baldwin Sharknose so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Steam tractive effort + grade resistance (public-domain railroad formulas)
import math

def tractive_effort(cyl_dia_in, stroke_in, driver_dia_in, boiler_psi, factor=0.85):
    # TE = 0.85 * P * d^2 * s / D  (simplified)
    return factor * boiler_psi * cyl_dia_in**2 * stroke_in / driver_dia_in

# Big Boy-ish: 23.75in bore... use class example 26x28, 68in drivers, 300 psi
te = tractive_effort(26, 28, 68, 300)
print(f"tractive effort: {te:,.0f} lb")

def grade_resistance(weight_tons, grade_pct):
    return weight_tons * 2000 * grade_pct / 100  # 20 lb/ton per % grade
train_tons = 4000
print(f"4000-ton train on 1% grade: {grade_resistance(train_tons, 1):,.0f} lb resistance")
print(f"can it climb? {'yes' if te > grade_resistance(train_tons, 1) else 'no'} "
      f"(TE {te:,.0f} vs {grade_resistance(train_tons, 1):,.0f})")

# Stopping: 60 mph, emergency ~ 1.5 mph/s decel
v_fps = 60 * 1.46667
print(f"emergency stop from 60mph: ~{v_fps**2/(2*1.5*1.46667):.0f} ft")
